title: What I Learned from Bryce Dallas Howard About Privilege
author: Graham, Molly
summary: Podcast host Molly Graham, granddaughter of Washington Post publisher Katharine Graham, describes a conversation with actor and director Bryce Dallas Howard, daughter of Ron Howard, in which both women's shared instinct to prove they 'earned' their success is challenged by a UC Berkeley rigged-Monopoly study showing that people randomly given advantages still construct stories about deserving their wins. Howard's reframe, accept that you didn't earn it, then ask what you'll do with what you were given, shifts the conversation from defending one's position to using inherited confidence, knowledge, and access to sponsor others, distinguishing sponsorship (using your name for someone not in the room) from mentorship (sharing advice). Graham argues nearly everyone inherits some unearned advantage, and the productive response is to spend energy deciding what to do next rather than defending how you got there.
points: Uses a UC Berkeley rigged-Monopoly experiment to show how people narrate advantage as merit even when it was randomly assigned.
Distinguishes 'mentorship' (sharing knowledge) from 'sponsorship' (spending your name and access on someone else's behalf).
Argues inherited advantage extends beyond wealth to confidence, insider knowledge, and family stability.
Reframes the useful question from 'did I earn this?' to 'what will I do with what I was given?'
quotes: Researchers brought pairs of strangers into a lab to play Monopoly. Before they started, they flipped a coin to decide which player would be "rich." That player got twice as much money to start, collected twice as much money when they passed Go, and got to roll two dice instead of one.
They had literally watched a coin flip give them a huge advantage, and they still told themselves a story about why they deserved to win.
She talked about the difference between mentorship and sponsorship: mentorship is sharing what you know; sponsorship is putting your name behind someone when they're not in the room.
Her point is that a much better question is "what am I going to do with what I was given?
You can spend your life defending your starting position, or you can spend it deciding what to do from here. Only one of those is actually in your control.
